questions.q: Summarize the paper's main contributions.

answer.text: The paper proposes a new network architecture called the Transformer, which relies solely on attention mechanisms and dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely [p. 1](#page=1). This new architecture achieves superior quality and is more parallelizable, requiring significantly less training time [p. 1](#page=1). The Transformer model achieves state-of-the-art BLEU scores on the WMT 2014 English-to-German and English-to-French translation tasks [p. 8](#page=8). It also generalizes well to other tasks, such as English constituency parsing [p. 10](#page=10). The code used to train and evaluate the models is available [p. 10](#page=10).

questions.q: What are the main ideas of this paper?

answer.text:
This paper introduces BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), a new language representation model that aims to improve fine-tuning based approaches for downstream tasks [p. 1](#page=1). BERT alleviates the unidirectionality constraint of previous models by using a "masked language model" pre-training objective, inspired by the Cloze task [p. 1](#page=1). This allows BERT to incorporate context from both directions, which is crucial for tasks like question answering [p. 1](#page=1).

The framework involves two steps: pre-training on unlabeled data and fine-tuning on labeled data for specific downstream tasks [p. 3](#page=3). BERT has a unified architecture across different tasks [p. 3](#page=3). The paper reports results on two model sizes: BERTBASE and BERTLARGE [p. 3](#page=3). BERTBASE has the same model size as OpenAI GPT, but uses bidirectional self-attention, whereas GPT uses constrained self-attention [p. 3](#page=3).

The paper also discusses fine-tuning BERT on various tasks, including Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST-2), Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA), Recognizing Textual Entailment (RTE), Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark (STS-B), and Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC) [p. 15](#page=15). Additionally, it mentions experiments on the SQuAD dataset for question answering [p. 7](#page=7) and the SWAG dataset for commonsense inference [p. 7](#page=7).

questions.q: Give an overview of this paper.

answer.text:
This paper introduces a deep residual learning framework to address the degradation problem in deep neural networks [p. 2](#page=2). Instead of fitting a desired underlying mapping $H(x)$, the framework explicitly lets stacked layers fit a residual mapping $F(x) := H(x) - x$, resulting in the formulation $F(x) + x$ [p. 2](#page=2), [p. 3](#page=3). This approach is motivated by the observation that deeper models can suffer from increased training error, a phenomenon the authors call the degradation problem [p. 2](#page=2), [p. 3](#page=3).

The paper proposes using "shortcut connections" to implement this residual learning [p. 2](#page=2). These connections, which skip one or more layers, are used to add the output of the residual mapping $F(x)$ to the input $x$ [p. 2](#page=2). Identity shortcut connections are presented as a parameter-free option that adds no computational complexity [p. 2](#page=2).

The authors present comprehensive experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets to evaluate their method [p. 2](#page=2), [p. 7](#page=7). They show that their residual networks (ResNets) can overcome the optimization difficulties faced by plain networks and achieve accuracy gains with increased depth [p. 7](#page=7). Notably, a 152-layer ResNet achieved a single-model top-5 validation error of 4.49% on ImageNet, outperforming previous ensemble results [p. 7](#page=7). An ensemble of six ResNet models won first place in the ILSVRC 2015 classification competition [p. 2](#page=2), [p. 7](#page=7). The paper also explores extremely deep models, including a 1202-layer network that achieved training error below 0.1% [p. 8](#page=8).

The paper also discusses related work on shortcut connections and bottleneck architectures [p. 2](#page=2), [p. 6](#page=6). They compare their identity shortcuts with projection shortcuts, finding that while projection shortcuts can be marginally better, identity shortcuts are crucial for not increasing the complexity of bottleneck architectures [p. 6](#page=6). The authors also analyze layer responses and find that ResNets generally have smaller responses, supporting the idea that residual functions are closer to zero than non-residual functions [p. 8](#page=8).

answer.text: ImageNet training starts with a learning rate of 0.1 [p. 4](#page=4), [p. 7](#page=7). This learning rate is divided by 10 at 32k and 48k iterations [p. 7](#page=7). For the 110-layer ResNet, the initial learning rate of 0.1 is found to be too large, so 0.01 is used to warm up the training until the training error is below 80%, after which it returns to 0.1 [p. 7](#page=7).

questions.q: What CIFAR-10 test error does the 110-layer ResNet reach?

answer.text: The 110-layer ResNet reaches a test error of 6.43% [p. 8](#page=8).

questions.q: What kind of building block do ResNet-50, 101 and 152 use?

answer.text: ResNet-50, 101, and 152 use a "bottleneck" building block [p. 6](#page=6). This bottleneck design consists of a stack of 3 layers: 1x1 convolution, 3x3 convolution, and another 1x1 convolution. The 1x1 layers are used to reduce and then restore dimensions, with the 3x3 layer acting as the bottleneck [p. 6](#page=6).

questions.q: Did the ImageNet models use dropout?

answer.text: The models were trained without dropout [p. 7](#page=7).

questions.q: What is the inner-layer dimensionality of the position-wise feed-forward networks?

answer.text: The inner-layer dimensionality of the position-wise feed-forward networks is $d_{ff} = 2048$ [p. 5](#page=5).

questions.q: How many identical layers make up the encoder stack?

answer.text: The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers [p. 3](#page=3).

questions.q: What beam size and length penalty were used for decoding?

answer.text: We used beam search with a beam size of 4 and length penalty $\alpha = 0.6$ [p. 8](#page=8). For the WSJ only and semi-supervised settings, we used a beam size of 21 and $\alpha = 0.3$ [p. 10](#page=10).

questions.q: How large is the WMT 2014 English-French dataset?

answer.text: The WMT 2014 English-French dataset consists of 36 million sentences [p. 7](#page=7).

questions.q: How many sentence pairs does the WMT 2014 English-German dataset have?

answer.text: The WMT 2014 English-German dataset consists of about 4.5 million sentence pairs [p. 7](#page=7).

questions.q: What scaling factor separates the paper's attention from plain dot-product attention?

answer.text: The scaling factor that separates the paper's attention from plain dot-product attention is $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ [p. 4](#page=4).

questions.q: What training cost in FLOPs does the results table list for GNMT + RL on English-to-German?

answer.text: The training cost in FLOPs for GNMT + RL on English-to-German is $2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ [p. 8](#page=8).
